amourAmi.r1_d: You care about this person, that much is obvious, but nothing in your answers looks like love: no jealousy when they tell you about their dates, no wish to kiss them, no "what if". What you have is a solid friendship, and those don't grow on trees.
amourAmi.r1_a: Hold on to it, and stop asking yourself the question every time someone says you would make a good couple. They are the ones projecting, not you.
amourAmi.r2_t: There's something, but it isn't love
amourAmi.r2_d: A few answers step outside friendship: a sting here, a comparison there. It isn't nothing, but it isn't the big thing either. Most likely, it's an attraction that comes and goes, the kind that exists in many very close friendships.
amourAmi.r2_a: No need to decide today. Watch what it does to you over a few weeks, without pushing one way or the other. If it grows, you will know. If it fades, you won't have broken anything.
amourAmi.r3_d: Your answers say something you probably already know: the wish to be close, the jealousy that stings, the others who no longer measure up. You are in the zone where friendship tips over, the one where you keep saying "my best friend" while feeling the word no longer fits.
amourAmi.r3_a: Two options, and both are defensible: talk about it, or let it pass by taking a little distance. What doesn't work is pretending nothing has changed. It shows, and it damages the friendship more surely than an honest conversation.
amourAmi.r4_t: You are in love, and you know it
amourAmi.r4_d: You have pictured what comes next, you have thought about kissing them, the idea of this person getting into a relationship tightens your stomach. This is no longer a friendship overflowing: these are feelings of love, whole ones.
amourAmi.r4_a: The question is no longer what you feel. It is what you do with it, and what the other person feels. Read their signals, pick a quiet moment, and if you decide to speak, do it simply, without a grand declaration.
